articles.summary: Revisiting Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas in 2026: the single bestselling game on the most successful console in the history of the business.
articles.body:
I’m taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t come with any new IGN score, but they will re-examine what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release. By the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly rank in my long-term love for this series.

Today it’s time to go home to Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas.

Whether you remember it or not – or were too preoccupied being spoon-fed puréed fruit from a jar at the time – it’s impossible to understate what a banner year 2004 was for now-legendary video games. Just look at the line up. World of Warcraft. Half-Life 2 and Halo 2. Burnout 3 and Metal Gear Solid 3. Gran Turismo 4 and more – much more. I could absolutely go on. To emerge as the bestselling game of what may well be the greatest year we’ve ever had – in an era where it felt like the rulebook was being torn up and rewritten every other month – you had to be remarkable. You had to be rich, surprising, innovative, and essential. Simply put, to be the bestselling game of 2004, you needed to be more than great. You needed to be Grand.

While GTA III defined the fundamentals of 3D open-world design, and Vice City layered that sandbox with vibrant ’80s style and a big dose of yacht rock and yayo, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas pushed the formula to the very limits of what was actually possible on the world’s then-favourite DVD player. Despite shipping just two years after Vice City, San Andreas expanded Rockstar’s formula exponentially by introducing three full-scale cities – all housed in what amounted to an entire fictional US state: the titular San Andreas. Best of all, it was still retro-tinged, set in 1992. A slightly less dramatic leap into the past than Vice City but, as someone whose adolescence was forged in the ’90s, an awesome period to revisit.

At the time, it was a mindblowing achievement. The state itself covers an area roughly six times larger than Vice City. Its three major metropolises – Los Santos, San Fierro, and Las Venturas – each have their own unique visual identity. Los Santos is draped in smog, giving the whole cityscape a distinct orange haze at certain times of day. On the hottest days, a shimmering heat rises from the asphalt – a fabulously effective flourish that gives the city a truly tangible sense of temperature. San Fierro, defined by its severe hills and stretches of tramline, features an entirely different sort of climate. It’s more akin to GTA III’s Liberty City, where the tall, dense skyscrapers of the CBD create quite a bit of shade below. Las Venturas, San Andreas’ gambling haven, is dry, flat, and is at its best at neon-lit night. Each city is connected by open stretches of rolling fields, redwood forests, and rocky desert. There’s even a selection of tiny towns, farms, and factories between the major hubs.

However, while the size of the map was one thing – the fact that you can travel all over it and move from one major city to another without a single loading screen is something else altogether. Coming from Vice City, where you couldn’t cross from one island to the other without being briefly stalled by a loading screen, it was a genuinely amazing advancement. Rockstar had concocted a way to constantly stream in the world immediately around us in real-time. For its debut on PS2 – the platform that accounted for more than 17 million of San Andreas’ 27.5 million sales – this meant a neverending juggling act with the system’s limited 32MB of RAM and a relentless assault on its disc drive. You probably could’ve forgiven the Rockstar North team for not adding a high-speed fighter jet to a game perpetually pulling data from its dual-layer DVD in a non-stop race against time to rapidly build the world in front of you before you reached it.

It’s arguable San Andreas’ greatest victory isn’t simply the immense geographical scale it boasted for its era. Rather, it’s the remarkable density of its various systems, ideas, and side activities.

I played an aggressive amount of San Andreas back in the mid 2000s. I tortured my PS2 until it started making weird noises, then I borrowed my sister’s and tortured it, too. Perhaps the ultimate testament to how supremely stuffed San Andreas is with things to do is just how many side modes I’ve encountered over the last week of playing that had honestly slipped my mind over the last 20 years. The valet activity? Forgot that. Trucking missions? Forgot those. Duelling lowriders? Oh, yeah! It’s like putting on an old pair of trousers and finding $20 notes in every pocket.

San Andreas almost never stops giving. Take its vehicles, for instance. Not only do they all handle with a genuine sense of heft that puts most GTA clones to shame – seriously, just watch as they subtly wiggle on their springs if you jerk them to a sudden halt – but there are also around 200 of them. From the minute it puts you on a bicycle, new vehicles are in virtually constant supply. Combine harvesters. Quad bikes. Articulated semi-trailers. Monster trucks. Functional forklifts. Hovercraft. A jump jet, and a jetpack. No, not one or the other. Both. It’s like someone took a bunch of scribbled brainstorm notes and executed on every suggestion, without trimming any of them.

To be honest, there are times playing San Andreas where it almost feels like no idea was trimmed. Rob a house, go dancing, and stop at a minimart to play an arcade machine. Hit the gym, then hit the casino. Run a triathlon, and run a business. Go parachuting, unwind with some pool, and… role play as a pimp. I guess, strictly speaking, there was at least one idea that was famously pulled out at the last minute: a sex minigame. It just wasn’t pulled out enough, so to speak. Ruled out so late in development it was impractical to completely remove it without jeopardising San Andreas’ vast, precarious, and otherwise interwoven code, Rockstar locked off the minigame beneath a non-interactive wrapper – keeping the camera entirely out of the room where the magic was happening. Modders discovered and re-enabled it in time for the PC version in 2005, triggering what became known as the Hot Coffee controversy.

The pearl clutching and hand wringing that followed was deeply embarrassing, even by mid 2000s standards. The US ESRB re-issued all versions of the game a commercially crippling Adults Only rating, and Australia temporarily banned it until the abandoned content was removed. It didn’t matter that it literally wasn’t even accessible for the majority of players on console – the matter had become politicised and the subject of massive media attention. The concept of two blocky PS2 characters goofily grinding against each other was apparently too much for adult gamers to bear. We would have to be content with wanton vehicular homicide and burning cops to a crisp. I’m hopeful that things would go a little differently more than two decades on, but I guess we have our own problems. These days I don’t know if I’m still killing people in video games, or if I’m only unaliving them.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas – The Legacy Review Screenshots

The explosion of side activities is still only part of the San Andreas equation, as Rockstar also introduced a number of light RPG mechanics. This goes beyond the ability to customise leading man Carl Johnson’s appearance, via outfits, haircuts, tattoos, or munching down too many burgers. CJ also has a large number of improveable skills, and the more you do something, the better and more efficient he’ll get at it. Flying, fighting, driving, diving – you name it. Have a weapon you prefer? Use it as much as possible to level CJ up to ‘Hitman’ proficiency, where you can move and strafe while shooting, your lock-on range will extend, and (in the case of the four specific weapons) even dual wield them.

The improvements to the third-person shooter component in San Andreas are significant, with most of the clumsiness that tended to characterise GTA III and Vice City ironed out. A bulk of that is thanks to the ability to finally use the right analogue stick to control the camera at will – as opposed to the previous games, where the right stick was only used to look around in a stationary first-person camera. It’s the first GTA game to feel akin to a modern third-person shooter in this regard, which makes it a breeze to get accustomed to in 2026. You can also aim all weapons freely now, rather than just a select few – and the auto lock-on is otherwise intelligent enough to automatically prioritise and target threats rather than random civilians or, worse, your own gang members. Light stealth was even introduced, on the back of Rockstar’s own experimentation with the controversial Manhunt earlier the same year. CJ is able to crouch to reduce noise, a suppressed pistol has been added to the arsenal, and there’s a simple stealth kill you can perform on the unaware, indicated by the same raised-arm trigger used in Manhunt.

With more cities, more cars, and more depth than ever, you might have been wondering just how much more more San Andreas could possibly have in store.

Well, I haven’t even touched on the radio stations yet, which are neck and neck with Vice City as the best they’ve ever been in the 30-year history of the series. It’s an impeccably curated soundtrack that’s one part perfect ’90s time capsule, and one part historical hip hop odyssey. That is, it didn’t just feature some of the most iconic rap tracks to emerge from the early ’90s, but it made sure to include stations dedicated to the entire ecosystem of complementary music hip hop found itself drawing inspiration from. Funk and soul. R&B and New Jack Swing. There’s perhaps no better example of that than the fact San Andreas didn’t make a choice between Charles Wright’s signature hit Express Yourself, or the 1988 reimaging from N.W.A. It simply included both. Eleven stations and over 150 songs is the bullet point, but there’s so much more to it than that. It’s the fact that they now air dynamically, meaning the song order changes and you won’t always hear the same slice of DJ banter introducing them.

Want more? Well, how about arguably the greatest arsenal of cheats codes ever assembled? Cheats to make the game easier. Cheats to make the game harder. Cheats to spawn all the greatest vehicles. Cheats to arm civilians with rocket launchers. Cheats to trigger a map-wide riot. Cheats to turn off the gravity!

Still want more? How about a same screen co-op mode that allows you to bring a friend into the world to wreak havoc alongside you. Is it slightly janky? Yes. Did that stop my friends and I from messing around with it constantly? Absolutely not.

Interestingly, about the only thing San Andreas seems to have fewer of is major Hollywood celebrities in the main roles. Following Vice City, San Andreas moved away from having a big-shot celebrity on deck to star as the lead character. Instead, CJ was capably and memorably played by an LA-based rapper named Young Maylay, with no previous acting experience. There are a number of recognisable names here as side characters, though, including James Woods, Peter Fonda, Charlie Murphy, Ice-T, Chris Penn, and the inimitable Sam Jackson as the iconically slimy Officer Frank Tenpenny. Is there a better GTA villain than Jackson’s Tenpenny? I don’t think there is.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is the single bestselling game on the most successful console in the history of the business. That’s not an accolade you can just earn by accident. Its unprecedented scope and astonishing depth were nothing short of witchcraft, and the incredible attention to detail was staggeringly impressive for something of its size. Its ability to support endless experimentation kept my friends and I busy for years, fooling around with its industry-leading list of cheats and its same-screen co-op chaos long after we’d all finished the story mode several times. Its soundtrack is the stuff of legend; so one-of-a-kind that not even Rockstar itself could quite reassemble the complete thing for subsequent re-releases. In 2004, GTA San Andreas was one of the most extraordinary games I’d ever played. In 2026, the hood done took me under all over again. Sure, the technical limitations of the mid 2000s are always obvious through a modern lens, but you can’t measure ambition in polygons – and GTA San Andreas is overflowing with it.

For more reflections on the incredible Grand Theft Auto series, you can read our new Legacy Reviews of Grand Theft Auto , Grand Theft Auto 2 , Grand Theft Auto III , and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City , with more to follow before November.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve Review
articles.summary: The best aerial combat the series has ever had alongside some of its best mission design.
articles.body:
Editor's Note: This review currently only covers Ace Combat 8's single-player campaign, as reviewers were given a very limited amount of time with its multiplayer modes ahead of release. It will be updated with a finalized score and multiplayer impressions once we put the PvP through its paces on live servers.

There’s a theory that it’s impossible to make a piece of anti-war art set during a war – that, no matter what you do, the work itself inevitably becomes (or will be interpreted as) pro-war. I’m sympathetic to the argument; Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is a war story about how awesome it is to be a heroic ace pilot. It is also unapologetically anti-war and plays with complex ideas like the role of propaganda, the power of symbols, nationalism and globalism. And it extends to the way corporations influence and manipulate world events, social media and the rise of news that may or may not be real, the price and horrors of war, and what a world without borders might look like. Its story is often startlingly relevant, but when I think about my time with it, my mind returns to a single thought: Wings of Theve’s never directly stated but deeply held belief that the best thing that could happen to this world and its characters would be for the war to be over, and for none of them to ever fly a combat mission again. It marries exceptional air combat with a melodramatic but moving story, one of the year’s best soundtracks, and incredible visual design to make a war game that never lets you forget how terrible everything happening here is.

Wings of Theve takes place about ten years after Ace Combat 7 , though you don’t need to be familiar with its predecessor to enjoy it. The Republic of Sotoa launches a blitzkrieg invasion of the Federation of Central Usea using the power of its air force and orbital missiles strikes known as Tonitrus Spears. The FCU capital of Theve falls. Shattered and broken, what’s left of the FCU fights a hopeless, defensive war from the deck of the Endurance, an aging aircraft carrier that, in better times, would have probably ended up as a museum, but the crew of the Endurance fights on. Your character, a nameless fighter pilot, is fished out of the ocean by one of the Endurance’s rescue helicopters, and you’re quickly assigned to fly second seat to Jan “Rex” Cope, the legendary Wings of Theve, the FCU’s ace of aces.

Trouble is, it’s all a lie. Cope is an exceptional pilot, but he’s never shot anyone down. His kill count is a myth, fabricated to give the people of Usea hope. As long as the Wings of Theve is in the skies, the story goes, the fight isn’t over. Cope’s job is to bring his squadron, Joker Flight, back with him. And he’s done it well. But his luck runs out when you run into Sotoan ace Shadow 22. But the Wings of Theve cannot die, so you inherit the mantle and Cope’s old callsign. You have become the name. And when legend becomes fact, print the legend and watch it go viral on social media. But it’s not enough for Joker Flight to just run anymore. They need to produce results. And as you start to shoot down enemy fighters, the lines between the legend of the Wings of Theve and reality start to blur.

It’s a compelling yarn that developer Project Aces has spun, and it unravels into an earnest story with the Joker Flight crew at its heart. Baxter (callsign “Professor”) is a former teacher turned pilot, mentor to the other members of Joker Flight, and your wingman; Tasha, Joker Flight’s youngest member, a generationally-talented civvie stunt pilot forced into service by the war who refuses to shoot anyone down; and Coster (callsign “Noise”), a quiet rock and roll enthusiast who manages to fly Tasha’s wing while blasting tunes over your comms. Many other supporting characters feed into the myth of the Wings of Theve whether it be your commanding XO, your Queen Flight counterparts, or the media machine spinning you up. And through it all, the legend of Cope (and his spirit) lingers.

Maybe that sounds silly, but like everything else in Wings of Theve, it works surprisingly well and allows you to continue to build a connection to a character whose life and death are crucial to Wings of Theve’s world. And make no mistake, it is Wings of Theve’s characters that make this story work. They’re well-drawn, complex, interesting people elevated by genuinely excellent performances from the voice cast and your relationships with these characters drive much of Wings of Theve’s story. Whenever we sortied, I wanted to make sure I brought them home.

Ace Combat has long told its story from inside the cockpit, but Wings of Theve also puts your character on the Endurance’s deck, inside the mess with your fellow pilots and civvies who have sought refuge on the carrier, and inside hangars briefing rooms, among other places. These moments help you connect with the members of Joker Flight and the other people aboard the Endurance, but they also drive home the cost of the war, and make it feel like this world exists outside of the cockpit. You can’t really do much during them except look around and perform simple interactions, but they're home to some of Wings of Theve’s most memorable and affecting moments.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve - June 2026 Screenshots

Ultimately, though, you’re a combat pilot; your place is in the air. And it’s here that Ace Combat soars (sorry), expertly weaving its story, moment-to-moment gameplay, and mission design into masterful, elegant maneuvers worthy of a state-of-the-art fighter jet. Like its predecessors, Wings of Theve is a mission-based game. After you’ve been briefed on your next sortie, you’ll select your aircraft, weapons, and parts – which you can buy (along with new planes) with points you earn by completing missions. All that affects everything from how many missiles or special weapons you can equip or how much damage they do to how well your plane handles. You can even outfit your crew’s planes if you want (or have them auto-assigned something that fits the mission at hand). Then you’re airborne, and it’s time to fly.

Often, things start pretty simply. Maybe you need to defend the Endurance, assault an air field, protect a friendly plane, or take out some transports. But these initial objectives are just a reason to take to the air. The beauty of Ace Combat has always been in its flying, when the infinite possibilities of the skies above intersect with the limitations of your aircraft and the realities of your mission. You could play with the standard controls, which substantially limit your aircraft, but you should absolutely play with the Expert scheme if you can. The joy lives in the complete control of the pitch, roll, and yaw of your plane, simultaneously opening you to rapturous moments of aviation choreography and shattering mistakes when you misjudge a turn or your altitude resulting in a devastating crash.

You find yourself in small moments: in the high-G turns to evade incoming missiles, locking onto a group of planes with a special anti-air weapon and knocking four of them out of the sky at once, or deftly weaving through a city and over debris. Wings of Theve captures the fighter pilot fantasy when you're getting on a target's six and downing them with a perfectly placed series of machine gun shots or in finding just the right air speed to stay behind a massive transport before turning your nose and shredding its engines with your guns without ever firing a missile.

You can be perfect in Wings of Theve if you try, and that's when pilot and aircraft merge and flight becomes an extension of human expression in spite of the limitations of weight and gravity. Each moment and small choice builds the future of your sortie in real time. It's in tailing a Sotoan plane, your reticle turning red, the lock on tone roaring in your ears, and launching a missile and watching it arc elegantly into the other plane’s fuselage before flying through the wreckage in search of your next target. Destruction as beauty. Wings of Theve consistently delivers on this thrill, and it is exhilarating each time.

But what is remarkable is how Wings of Theve marries these moments with its mission design and story. Sometimes, you’ll have your targets marked for you, but often it's on you and the rest of Joker Flight to figure out where to be. Maybe your radar is jammed, and you can’t track the transport planes you need to shoot down, so you’ll need to pick out the contrails they leave behind among the clouds and follow them. Or perhaps a ground detachment is under attack, and calls for aid on your radio. You’ll have to figure out where that detachment is, what you need to target to help, and how to approach it. Can they hold position for a minute while you handle threats elsewhere? Do you dispatch Joker Flight to help, authorizing the use of their limited special weapons, or keep them flying close formation to cover you and try to do it yourself? Missions in Wings of Theve change constantly, and your objectives will change depending on the state of the battlefield. It is a brilliant, graceful ballet where new dancers constantly take the stage, and you must improvise the steps accordingly.

My favorite missions put the ball in Joker Flight’s court. In one, we had to fight off a Sotoan land battleship (think a battleship with tank treads). As we dodged fire from its massive railguns, we also had to cover our ground troops and take out its weapons. It was a tough fight; I’d brought bombs that excelled at destroying its weapons but struggled when we needed precision targeting near the armor around its treads. In another mission, we had to take out airships that helped Sotoa target its Tonitrus Spears. They were hidden in the clouds and invisible from radar, so between fending off air attacks on the Endurance’s fleet, we would follow the massive lasers that guided the Spears once the airships aimed at their targets, and destroy them before they annihilated our fleet.

All of this is brilliant stuff that tests not only your ability to pick the right aircraft and weapons for the job – though you could stick with the capable default F/A-18C, just not as impressive as my beloved F-22A, for example. But it's also about responding on the fly to dynamic objectives that may be very different from your original briefing and the mission you’d planned for. I’ve stuck mostly to talking about the first half of Wings of Theve’s 30 missions here to avoid spoilers, but every single one is excellent, and the final missions pull out all the tricks for some genuinely showstopping moments.

Wings of Theve’s narrative triumph is in portraying most of its drama through the calls coming in over your comms. When your forces are taking heavy losses, some soldiers will urge their comrades to fight on because the Wings of Theve is protecting them, while others will question your usefulness or if the stories about you are even true. You’ll hear men and women die in combat because you weren’t fast enough or just couldn’t protect them. Joker and Queen Flights will react to what’s happening in real time. “Hello traitors, did the wicked get their rest?” Tasha will taunt a former FCU squadron now fighting for Sotoa. Coster will play music to inspire the rest of the crew, and you may end up flying with the guys who recorded it. Sotoan forces will come through on your radio, calling out for their friends as you shoot them down, talking strategy, or taunting you. And then the Shadows themselves might announce their presence by singing over an open channel – that’s when you know you’re in for a serious dogfight (I still can’t get that tune out of my head).

All of this combines with standard combat chatter, but it’s never overbearing as you’ll always know what’s happening. It’s a remarkable achievement in audio mixing, and more impressive that Wings of Theve manages to tell a compelling, emotional story this way. Like previous games in the series, Wings of Theve is a melodrama, and that might turn some folks off, but I found it exceptionally compelling and full of pathos. It’s most effective in its smallest moments – when Tasha confronts the cost of her pacifism, or when Coster gets to meet his musical heroes in the skies. And it extends to just the banter between the crew that fills the quiet moments before or after a mission.

When we had to listen to FCU ground forces calling for help and reporting their losses, wondering aloud if Wings had abandoned them, I felt bad. Keeping them safe was my responsibility, but much of what happens in any given mission is out of your control, no matter how well you fly. That’s war, but it always made me try harder, fly better, and refocus. I had to live up to the legend, whether it was true or not. And while shooting down Sotoan forces and watching them realize they had no chance in real-time was satisfying, it was essy to understand their anger over what had happened to their comrades or their fear when we turned the tide. As exhilarating as being a fighter pilot is, Wings of Theve never lets you forget that everything happening here is a tragedy. And it doesn’t shy away from portraying the toll of war not just on the people forced to fight it, but on civilians who live through it, too. There is a cost to all of this, and the storytelling drives that home every time it can. And yet, you can’t help but want to be everything the Wings of Theve are cracked up to be, to instill hope for desperate people fighting for their right to live free of oppression. Every time I climbed into the cockpit, Wings of Theve reminded me that I was a symbol, more powerful than any combination of pilot or plane could ever aspire to be. The challenge was to live up to it.

Some of my favorite moments in Ace Combat 8 are when there’s no fighting: flying through immaculately rendered clouds, drops of rain speckling my canopy, or landing on the Endurance or at an airstrip after a job well done, or unlocking a new plane and watching the massive hanger doors open and light spill across its sleek lines for the first time. There’s something beautiful about skimming the clouds and basking in the sun in a sky free of missiles and machine gun fire. While you can replay missions and aim for higher scores and S-ranks like me, Ace Combat is kind enough to let you fly around any map peacefully once you’ve completed its associated mission. Cope understood that feeling; maybe it’s why he never shot anyone down. And the longer I played Ace Combat 8, the more I understood him. Maybe he had it right all along.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is a remarkable achievement for Project Aces. It combines stunning visuals and sound design (seriously, Bandai Namco, please sell this soundtrack) with engaging story moments, whether they're out-of-the-cockpit sequences or the radio chatter that build up its excellent, memorable characters. It's also a surprisingly emotional and resonant story that's deeply relevant to the current age while delivering the best aerial combat the series has ever had alongside some of its best mission design. I haven’t been able to stop thinking about it since I stepped out of the cockpit for the last time, and I know the Wings of Theve, and their story, will stick with me for a very long time. For now, perhaps it's enough to hope for a world free of nations and war, one where we soar the skies freely for ourselves. And like the Wings of Theve, by believing in it, perhaps we can make it real.

articles.title: Marvel Launches Star-Studded 'Turn Off Your Phones' Theater Ad Featuring Your Favorite Avengers and X-Men
articles.summary: Before the multiverse collapses and Doctor Doom takes his throne, here's one last bit of Marvel fun: the cast of Avengers: Doomsday reuniting for a theater ad telling you to silence your cellphone.
articles.body:
Before the multiverse collapses and Doctor Doom takes his throne, here's one last bit of Marvel fun: the cast of Avengers: Doomsday reuniting for a theater ad telling you to silence your cellphone.

This brief promo has begun airing in theaters this week alongside the release of Avengers: Endgame Encore, which also features additional footage shot during the production of Avengers: Doomsday .

Many of Doomsday's biggest names (but not Robert Downey Jr.) return here for this silly skit, as members of the Avengers, New Avengers, X-Men and Fantastic Four settle down to catch a movie while all in costume. Unfortunately, someone's smartphone promptly rings, causing everyone to complain. "No, no, no!" shouts Yelena. And that's about it.

WE GOT TO SEE A NEW AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY “SILENCE YOUR PHONES” AD RIGHT BEFORE ENCORE!! #AvengersDoomsday #AvengersEndgameEncore pic.twitter.com/PeKvSrqMFh — ❤️ Ⓜ︎ᗩᗪD̸𝕆乂✨ (@TheMaddox08) September 24, 2026

WE GOT TO SEE A NEW AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY “SILENCE YOUR PHONES” AD RIGHT BEFORE ENCORE!! #AvengersDoomsday #AvengersEndgameEncore pic.twitter.com/PeKvSrqMFh

While brief, it's still remarkable to see such a lineup of comicbook heroes all in one shot — perhaps the most since Endgame's infamous portals scene.

Included in the ad are Channing Tatum's Gambit, Letitia Wright's Shuri, Florence Pugh's Yelena, Simu Liu's Shang-Chi, James Marsden's Cyclops, Pedro Pascal's Mr. Fantastic, Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm, Chris Hemsworth's Thor, Anthony Mackie's Captain America, David Harbour's Red Guardian, Sebastian Stan's Bucky, Wyatt Russell's John Walker, Hannah John-Kamen's Ghost, Rebecca Romijn's Mystique, Torres and Tenoch Huerta's Namor.

If you're settling down to watch Avengers: Endgame Encore this weekend, you'll know there are several additional scenes to also enjoy. But if you'd like more detail now on what these are, we have them all covered right here . Meanwhile, earlier today, we reported on new comments from Avengers director Anthony Russo discussing how Endgame Encore now leads directly into Avengers: Doomsday's storyline .

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: I Am Very Tired of Insomniac’s Approach to Marvel Supervillains
articles.summary: I am very tired of Insomniac’s approach to Marvel supervillains, and it makes less sense than ever in Wolverine.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Carlos Morales. He’s read several thousand Marvel comics and gets annoyed when adaptations don’t feel true to the characters.

Warning: this article contains spoilers for Marvel’s Wolverine.

Marvel’s Wolverine is out in the wild, marking the fourth collaboration between Insomniac Games and Marvel. But instead of being a triumphant new entry in the studio’s catalog, Wolverine has had a shaky launch, scoring a 6/10 in IGN’s official review and being savaged by online commenters . While the game isn’t as bad as the worst of the backlash would have you believe – a 6 on the IGN scale means ‘okay’, after all – it doesn’t reach the heights of Insomniac’s best games. It also highlights one of the studio’s most frustrating trends endemic to its triple-A Marvel games: the way it adapts supervillains from the Marvel universe.

All four of Insomniac’s Marvel games feature a story where the main villain is a close friend of the hero, and their falling out is the main source of the conflict. Not only is it unimaginative to keep recycling the same plot, but the recurring use of the trope has reached a new level of absurdity in Marvel’s Wolverine because it tries to tell that story with Mr. Sinister, one of Marvel’s most sociopathic antagonists. Let’s delve into why Insomniac needs a new approach to supervillains.

Marvel’s Wolverine establishes an odd status quo for mutants in the world of Insomniac’s Marvel games. There are no X-Men, and Nathaniel Essex, who in the comics is traditionally the supervillain Mr. Sinister, has led the covert Team X for almost 30 years. The game opens with Essex meeting a feral Wolverine, and much of the game’s first half is spent elaborating on their shared history. Logan credits Essex with saving his life and giving him purpose, a role that in most other versions is played by Professor X. Fans of the source material figured that a twist revealing Essex’s true nature would come, and it certainly does, but the way the game executes that plot turn is muddied by how Essex is portrayed early on.

Essex is not just Logan’s friend and commander of Team X. He’s also a mutant rights activist on a crusade to make the world safe for mutants by fighting Bolivar Trask and the Reavers. Although it’s later revealed that Essex lied about being a mutant and stole the X-gene from his wife Rebecca using mad science back in the 1800s, he still spends most of the game acting like a righteous champion of mutantkind. His plan to awaken dormant mutants using Sentinels powered by the Helix Engine (and killing any humans who happen to be in the way) feels like a scheme better suited to Magneto than Mr. Sinister.

You could argue that this is a new take on Essex and shouldn’t be judged against his comic persona, but that idea falls apart when the game does have him take on his comic appearance and personality for the final level. He threatens global armageddon by unleashing a fleet of gigantic Helix Sentinels and wants to absorb all mutant X-genes into himself, but there’s no coherent development between his “I want to save mutantkind” and “I will kill everyone on Earth” mindsets.

The beginning of the conflict between Logan and Essex also falls flat because it’s largely predicated on Essex being “too violent” in his methods before he turns into an omnicidal maniac at the very end. There’s a pivotal scene where Essex tortures Trask telekinetically despite Logan’s protests, so Logan mercy kills Trask to stop his suffering. This distinction in the degrees of violence feels arbitrary when Logan spends the whole game shredding hundreds if not thousands of people with his claws, often tearing his enemies apart in brutally painful ways. Was the reveal that Essex wiped Logan’s memories and reduced him to a feral state at the start of the game not enough to spark their divide? Weirdly, that’s one of the most on-brand moments for Essex despite the developers’ odd refusal to let him fully resemble his villainous alter ego.

Insomniac’s attempt to create an emotional falling out storyline between Logan and Essex struggles because it requires turning Essex into a completely different character from his comic incarnation. If you’re not familiar with Mr. Sinister in the comics, he started as a scientist in the 19th century who became obsessed with eugenics and mutation. He was granted superpowers and immortality by fellow X-Men villain Apocalypse, and would later become one of the team’s greatest foes, as well as developing a special enmity with Cyclops and Jean Grey. Sinister has no illusions about the morality of his work; he calls himself Mr. Sinister , after all. He’s in it for science and satisfaction, and given all he’s done (including working with the Nazis in World War 2), there are few Marvel villains less suited to a more sympathetic portrayal.

So while fans of the source material will likely find Essex being a mutant crusader confusing, newcomers to the character won’t understand why he goes full dark side at the end when he spends so much of the game touting the need to protect mutants. The game hints at a way to resolve this friction, but doesn’t actually make the connection: Apocalypse. The mutant megavillain is a major part of the game’s backstory, having turned Logan into his Horseman of Death many years ago. It’s even implied, but not stated, that Apocalypse gave Logan his adamantium skeleton instead of the Weapon X project. Apocalypse speaks to Logan in his mind multiple times, but doesn’t make a physical appearance aside from being in shadow in the post-credits scene. Since he’s an important (if unseen) part of Wolverine’s story, I can’t help but ask: why isn’t Apocalypse in league with Essex?

Although Sinister and Apocalypse have a long history in the comics, Essex in the game doesn’t seem to know who Apocalypse is, nor is it apparent that Apocalypse is influencing him from afar. Essex killing his wife to harvest her X-gene and psychically torturing Logan to remove his memories proves that Essex has been evil from the start, but if that’s the case, why was he acting like he was on the side of the angels for close to three decades? Why would he work so hard to show he cares about the welfare of mutants, to the point of trying to convince Logan of the righteousness of his actions even while laying siege to Madripoor? It almost feels like Essex is pursuing a greater goal that’s never made clear, but if Apocalypse was secretly ordering Essex to do all this, or if Essex knew of Apocalypse’s existence and was working against him by creating an army of mutants, a lot of Essex’s characterization starts to make more sense. Instead, we’re left with an unconvincing conflict between two “friends” that can’t land its emotional beats because there isn’t enough foundation to support it.

On a more basic level, it’s also just not very fun to have a Mr. Sinister who doesn’t get to embrace the flamboyant villainy of his namesake. The game never even calls him Sinister – his name is always Essex in dialogue. Even the name on the health bar during his boss fight is Essex. It feels like Insomniac took Mr. Sinister and bent him out of shape to suit its story instead of writing a story that suited him. Sadly, this has been standard operating procedure for the studio for some time.

One of the reasons that Marvel’s Spider-Man is the best Marvel game ever made is that it told a surprisingly heartfelt story that flipped the typical Spider-Man and Doctor Octopus relationship on its head. In Insomniac’s universe, Otto Octavius started not as one of Peter Parker’s greatest enemies, but as his mentor, with Peter working on robotic prosthetics with Otto between superhero missions. The genuine bond between the pair was tragically corrupted by Otto’s desire for revenge against Norman Osborn and the psychological damage that using the tentacle apparatus did to his mind. It’s a very different take on the source material, but it works because it doesn’t fundamentally change who Doctor Octopus is. He’s always been a dark reflection of the man Peter could be if he took his academic gifts and used them for villainy instead of heroism. It also plays perfectly into Peter’s understandable desire for a father figure after the death of Uncle Ben, with Peter needing to accept that he has to make his own choices instead of emulating idols who can disappoint him.

However, this alternate take on one of Marvel’s greatest villains had an unfortunate consequence: it worked so well that Insomniac has tried to replicate it in each subsequent game. The Tinkerer in Miles Morales, Venom in Spider-Man 2, and now Sinister in Wolverine are all former friends of each game’s protagonist, and all these stories are made worse by trying to redo what worked in the studio’s first Spider-Man. Phin Mason, aka the Tinkerer, is a supergenius friend of Miles who wants to attack the Roxxon Corporation, and falls into the all too common stereotype of leftist coded villains who have a “point” but are too cool with murder and therefore defined as evil by the plot. Her master plan to destroy Roxxon HQ puts all of Harlem in danger, and while the game tries to handwave this by saying she was unaware of the real blast radius because of a miscalculation, that’s an attempt to salvage her morals that also makes her look like an idiot. She also dies to get “redeemed,” which makes the whole arc feel pointless.

Harry Osborn is turned into Venom in Spider-Man 2, and while Harry is not traditionally one of the hosts of the Venom symbiote, the idea was at least foreshadowed in the previous game because of the symbiote being inside of his recuperation chamber. Yet his transformation into Venom makes no sense. He wears the symbiote with no ill effects for a while before giving it to Peter, who immediately turns into a dick because of the suit’s influence, and when Harry gets the symbiote back he transforms into a monster who doesn’t share his motivations. Sure, Venom claims he wants to “heal the world” because that’s something Harry said before, but he’s actually trying to conquer the world with a symbiote army, and the final boss fight makes it clear that Harry is basically a prisoner of the suit instead of being responsible for his actions, rendering the supposed tragedy of the conflict inert.

These diminishing returns hit a new low in Wolverine, where Essex doesn’t have a clear motivation for putting up a charade of heroism for so long. Essex acts heroic only so there can be a “twist” later on that he’s not, and the multitude of scenes where Logan and Essex yell at each other after the reveal don’t feel like former friends who can no longer see eye to eye so much as the script feeling obligated to have dialogue scenes between major action setpieces. By the time we get to the final boss fight, Essex is gleefully reciting cliché after cliché about “I am the future!” and “You have no chance!”, creating a climax that can be enjoyable as spectacle but is devoid of depth. It’s a sad state of affairs given how long the game was in development and how much the studio was clearly passionate about the property.

This is not to say that future Insomniac Marvel collaborations are doomed, but if the studio wants to get back on top, it needs to take a hard look at its storytelling instincts. Hopefully by the time we get to Spider-Man 3, the Venom spin-off, or the X-Men game, Insomniac will learn that for supervillains, one size most definitely does not fit all.

Carlos Morales writes novels, articles, and Mass Effect essays. You can follow his fixations on Twitter .

articles.title: Pokémon TCG First Partner Illustration Collection Series 3 Is Back at Amazon Ahead of Prime Big Deal Days
articles.summary: Amazon has restocked the Pokémon TCG First Partner Illustration Collection Series 3 at market price. Here is where to buy the latest anniversary set.
articles.body:
Amazon has brought back stock of the Pokémon TCG First Partner Illustration Collection Series 3 , with the final entry in the collector-focused series currently available for $39.99.

That's a particularly interesting price with Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days event just around the corner. The two-day shopping event kicks off October 6, so if you're looking to pick up some Pokémon cards before the big sales event arrives, this is one worth keeping an eye on.

The First Partner Illustration Collection Series 3 is the final instalment in the series, rounding out the collection with nine starter Pokémon from Hoenn, Kalos, and Paldea. That means Treecko, Torchic, Mudkip, Chespin, Fennekin, Froakie, Sprigatito, Fuecoco, and Quaxly are all represented, completing the full 27-Pokémon starter lineup across all three collections.

Pokémon TCG: First Partner Illustration Collection—Series 3

Considering the first two First Partner Illustration Collection boxes were regularly selling for $50 or more after launch, $39.99 isn't a bad price if you're still looking to pick up Series 3. The current market price has also been hovering around the mid-$30 range before shipping , so Amazon's price is at least competitive with what you'll find elsewhere.

Each Series 3 collection includes a Pokémon TCG promo pack containing three of nine possible illustration rare-style cards, two booster packs from the Pitch Black and Chaos Rising expansions, and an exclusive sticker sheet.

The bigger appeal here is obviously completing the collection. Series 1 covered Kanto, Sinnoh, and Alola, while Series 2 moved on to Johto, Unova, and Galar. Series 3 brings things full circle with Hoenn, Kalos, and Paldea, giving collectors the opportunity to pick up all 27 First Partner Pokémon across the three releases.

Pokémon TCG: First Partner Illustration Collection—Series 2

It's also worth remembering that the original MSRP was just $14.99, so $39.99 is still considerably higher than what these were supposed to cost at launch. Pokémon TCG products have become notoriously difficult to find at MSRP, though, and these First Partner collections are no exception.

If you do buy from Amazon, make sure you're getting the listing sold and shipped by Amazon rather than jumping on a cheaper third-party listing. If you're hunting for more Pokémon TCG restocks, be sure to check out our custom Amazon search tracker . It's a useful way to make sure you're picking up sealed products that are actually "sold and shipped" directly by Amazon, rather than a third-party seller.

articles.body:
Batman Day may officially be behind us, but why celebrate the Dark Knight on just one day of the year? Humble Bundle is extending out the fun with its awesome Batman Day Comics Bundle , which runs for another 15 days as of the time of this writing.

For as low as $20, you can get 30 comics in total through this bundle, plus a DC Universe Infinite 30-day trial offer, which would all normally total $487 if bought separately. articles.body:
There are hundreds of cinematic chase sequences in video games and they can all trace their roots back to an unlikely source. The colourful cartoon platformer that started it all: Crash Bandicoot.

The running-towards-camera chase sequence is as popular now as it’s ever been, raising the cinematic tension in blockbuster games for the last 30 years. articles.title: How One Crash Bandicoot Level Helped Build Naughty Dog
articles.summary: From a quick-fix solution to a triple-A staple, this is how an early Crash Bandicoot level inspired decades of cinematic level design in Uncharted and beyond.
articles.body:
As Leon Kennedy, we fled from a giant, mechanical statue. Eleven years later, we guided Nathan Drake and his brother, Sam, as they escaped from relentless pursuers on a motorbike . And recently, we helped forge a path through a literal wave of plague-infested rats for A Plague Tale’s Amicia . Three examples from literally hundreds of cinematic chase sequences in video games that can all trace their roots back to an unlikely source. The colourful cartoon platformer that started it all: Crash Bandicoot .

The running-towards-camera chase sequence is as popular now as it’s ever been, raising the cinematic tension in blockbuster games for the last 30 years. But its beginnings were humble, and its widespread use is all thanks to the Crash developers at Naughty Dog trying to solve a single problem: How do we show our character’s face more?

From a quick-fix solution to a triple-A staple, this is how an early Crash Bandicoot level inspired decades of cinematic level design.

Boulders is the fourth level in Crash Bandicoot, and takes the average player around 60 seconds to complete. Nestled amongst 31 other levels featuring lengthy side-scrolling gauntlets, tricky platforming, and painful difficulty spikes to overcome, it would be easy to assume that a quick, minute-long chase sequence wouldn’t be a particular highlight. But Boulders was the first of its kind. Any video game sequence where a character is chased towards the camera can trace its origins back to Crash Bandicoot. Perhaps the series it informed the most, though, was Naughty Dog’s own Uncharted series, which features multiple sequences of Nathan Drake running towards the camera across the entire series, as if it were a mandatory part of a Naughty Dog game’s DNA. Uncharted makes no secret of this fact. Long after Crash’s creators had left the company, Naughty Dog still paid homage to Boulders in Uncharted 4, when Nathan Drake was able to pick up the pad himself and experience the level firsthand.

“It’s the modern Naughty Dog playing the antique Naughty Dog.” said Jason Rubin, a co-creator of Crash Bandicoot, in a 2019 interview with IGN . “What Nathan’s doesn’t understand is that this is basically the game that led to you. You exist because of this game!”

The level design for Boulders began its journey in 1994. Naughty Dog, then a small independent studio fresh off the modestly performing Way of the Warrior, was ready to take the next step. And the soon-to-launch Sony PlayStation gave it a platform to try something no one had done before: create the first great 3D platformer. Super Mario 64 was still two years away and under lock and key, so the genre's rules were yet to be established by the king of platformers. Crash creators and Naughty Dog founders Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin saw an opportunity to stake their claim in the burgeoning genre. They immediately got to work, experimenting with how platforming could work in 3D, but they soon ran into an issue.

“We were trying to preserve all of the good elements of classic platform games,” explained Gavin in his 2016 blog post. “To maintain a solid control feel, we kept the camera relatively stable and oriented the control axis relative to the camera. This may seem obvious, but it wasn't at the time, and many 3D games used different (and usually inferior) schemes.”

“What would it be really like to do a platformer in 3D?” Gavin later said in a 2020 interview with Ars Technica . “Imagine you're going through loops like in Sonic the Hedgehog, or you're jumping platforms or collecting stuff in 3D. The camera's always behind you. All you do is see Sonic's ass, but the front of the character is where the expression is.” Locking the camera behind the character is now a tried-and-true method, used in almost all third-person action games today. But Gavin and Rubin were concerned this perspective would limit the character’s ability to connect with players – a thought that was particularly troubling considering the technical hurdles the team had overcome to bring Crash’s expressions to life.

“When Crash pulls his flat face out of the sand, shakes it off, looks confused, leaps up, looks at the camera and does his great big goofy smile… that sold Crash as a character,” explained Rubin. “No 2D game could afford the art, and no other 3D game had the facial animation that our system brought. And thus the main character transformed from an emotionless ‘vehicle’ to an emotive friend.”

The team at Naughty Dog knew their character was something special, and his ability to emote and react like a Looney Tunes cartoon separated them not only from the current competition, but eventually even Super Mario 64, the competition they didn’t even know they had. For this advantage to work, though, they needed to find more ways to get Crash’s face front and center.

“Our solution, which evolved over the next two years, was multi-fold,” shared Gavin in his blog post. “First, the character would start the game facing the screen. Second, we added 2D levels that guaranteed quality gameplay and a chance to see the character in a familiar pose, allowing comparison against old 2D games. And third, we would attempt the reverse of a Sonic ass level – the run INTO the screen.”

A desire to show more of Crash’s face led the developers to make their first breakthrough into cinematic territory and, ultimately, create the blueprint for Crash Bandicoot’s most iconic perspective. The angle switch, though, led to another issue. In the “Sonic’s ass” levels, players were always presented with the oncoming threat on the horizon. Despite the level of challenge, the linear path always gave players the intel they needed to progress – ensuring that any failure was the fault of the player’s ability, rather than the game design. When you stripped that intel away, you lost a core fundamental of the design. Players were now running into the unknown, so the obstacle path had to be light and forgiving. Much like other 3D games of the era, where open spaces became detrimental to conflict, Crash’s front-facing levels had, through necessity, been stripped of any challenge or drama.

“In 3D [platforming], you can just go to the right and avoid [enemies] entirely,” Gavin told Ars Technica. “You’ve added a whole dimension to the space, so now there’s too much empty space. It diluted the ratio between choice and conflict. We had to figure out how to compensate for this to maintain the action pace.”

“With all our technical and art successes, the game could not have succeeded without good gameplay,” shares Rubin. “This was by far the hardest part of making Crash Bandicoot.”

“We had this realisation that basically we had added a dimension, so the simplest strategy was to take out a dimension in some way,” said Gavin. “An example of that was the boulder level: the dimension we're actually taking out there is time.”

The solution was to use time to dictate Crash’s running speed. To increase the tension, Crash could no longer leisurely navigate the path. Naughty Dog looked to cinema for inspiration, and settled on Indiana Jones’ iconic boulder escape as the device to help force the player into a time-pressured environment vital to maintaining the desired level of conflict

“All this became the legendary boulder levels,” said Gavin in his blog post. “Apeing that moment from Raiders of the Lost Ark when the giant stone ball starts rolling toward Indy.”

The combination of character and conflict gave birth to the Crash Bandicoot chase sequence. Its immediate success cemented the form as not only a Crash Bandicoot staple, but also the cinematic inspiration for both Naughty Dog titles and other developers’ action games for years to come.

But Boulders' influence wasn’t limited to presentation. Crash Bandicoot arrived at the tail end of an era of punishing difficulty. In a time when arcade was king, most casual players couldn't finish a game, and game design often targeted difficulty to drive revenue. A failed run led to another coin in the slot, after all. But despite making sure Crash had its fair share of difficulty, Rubin and Gavin also wanted to create an approachable game – one that challenged skilled players but accommodated beginners and, perhaps more importantly, children.

“We realised that if a novice player died a lot of times, we could give them an Aku Aku at the start of a round and they had a better chance to progress,” explained Rubin. “We also figured out that if you died a lot while running from the boulder, we could slow it down a little each time. If you died too much, a fruit crate would suddenly become a continue point. Eventually everyone succeeded at Crash.”

It’s in this approach that you can see how, alongside scripted cinematic sequences, Crash Bandicoot also helped introduce another major video game design philosophy. Adaptive difficulty had been experimented with before, but in 1996, alongside the launch of Resident Evil, the background act of monitoring a player’s performance and adapting the game’s challenges to accommodate really began to take shape. The medium began to move away from punishing players for quarters to creating a dynamic experience that could tailor itself to your skill level.

Crash Bandicoot was an overwhelming success on the PlayStation. The small team of developers managed to birth a PlayStation icon who’s still celebrated 30 years later, and laid the foundation for Naughty Dog to become the renowned, elite developer we know today.

“I think we sold under 100,000 copies of Way of the Warrior, shared Rubin. “We sold 9 million copies of Crash.”

“Crash Bandicoot was really the crucible in which the Naughty Dog philosophy was forged,” said Gavin. “We wanted to make a truly great game that was gonna be a classic, and to do that, we came to believe everything in it had to be great.”

Naughty Dog exists today because of the risks taken on Crash Bandicoot. Their desire to show off impressive 3D facial animations led to a reinvention of platforming perspective, inspired a generation of chase sequences, and, perhaps most importantly, sparked Naughty Dog’s cinematic ambitions.

Dale Driver is an Associate Director of Video Programming at IGN, and once skipped revising for his exams so he could dedicate all his time to getting 120 stars in Mario 64. Be thoroughly bored by following him on Bluesky at @daledriver.bsky.social

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering's The Hobbit Booster Boxes Secure a New Price Cut Ahead of Prime Day
articles.summary: Amazon discounted MTG: The Hobbit Play Booster Boxes ahead of its next Prime Day sale. This is the best price we've seen on Hobbit boosters so far, with them effectively down to $5.66 per pack.
articles.body:
Magic: The Gathering waits for no player, and its packed 2026 release schedule means I'm still catching my breath after Marvel Super Heroes . Now, we've recently headed back to Middle-earth for another Universes Beyond set , although this one is doing something a little different.

Not only does The Hobbit mark a return to Middle-earth following 2023's hugely popular The Lord of the Rings: Tales of Middle-earth, it also brings Magic back to a more traditional fantasy setting.

And if you're looking to pick up some packs, Amazon has discounted The Hobbit Booster Boxes ahead of its Prime Big Deal Day sale in early October.

The Hobbit - Play Booster Box (30 Packs)

Magic: The Gathering Universes Beyond Booster Boxes typically cost $209.70 for 30 packs, and The Hobbit has been particularly difficult to find at that price in the run-up to launch.

That's effectively $6.99 per pack, but this deal brings the box down to $169.99, or around $5.66 per pack instead.

You also get a foil box topper featuring a reprint from The Lord of the Rings set, complete with special borderless alternate artwork.

The Most Valuable Hobbit Magic Cards So Far

Before we get into The Hobbit's priciest cards , there are a couple of caveats. We're using TCGplayer for pricing, and there's no value attached to The One Ring just yet.

More importantly, these are launch-day prices. Pre-release and early-market pricing can be extremely volatile, so don't expect these numbers to remain unchanged for long.

Still, if you're cracking packs over launch weekend, these are the cards you'll want to keep an eye out for.

The Arkenstone (Borderless) (Surge Foil)

Smaug, Wicked Worm (Borderless) (Surge Foil)
